title: The People With No Opinion
hook: Researchers looking for antidemocratic attitudes kept finding something else: not opposition, not support, but a shrug. They argue the shrug is what makes erosion possible.
key_points: 'Democratic neutrality' means expressing no opinion about politicians who undermine democratic norms — neither endorsing nor objecting.
The Notre Dame team pooled surveys of more than 48,000 Americans, fielded between September 2022 and July 2025.
At times 52% of voters expressed neutrality toward antidemocratic practices, while only about 8% openly backed making it harder for opponents to vote.
About 25% were neutral on whether politicians should put party loyalty ahead of the Constitution.
Taken together, nearly two-thirds expressed neutrality toward or support for at least one antidemocratic practice.
The authors' claim: neutrality is not a passive stance, because indifference removes the electoral cost of norm-breaking.
content_html: Surveys about threats to democracy usually count two groups: people who endorse antidemocratic behavior and people who condemn it. Writing in The Conversation, Matthew Hall, Brittany Solomon and Tyler Leigh of the University of Notre Dame's Rooney Democracy Institute argue that the most important group is the third one — the people who say they have no opinion at all.
extra_html:
Pooling surveys of more than 48,000 Americans fielded by YouGov, NORC and Bovitz between September 2022 and July 2025, they find that outright support for antidemocratic practices stays small: about 8% back making it harder for political opponents to vote. Neutrality is a different story. At points 52% of voters expressed no view on politicians who undermine democratic norms, and roughly a quarter were neutral on whether politicians should place party loyalty above the Constitution. Add the categories together and nearly two-thirds of respondents were either neutral toward or supportive of at least one antidemocratic practice, with about a third open to voting for a politician who prioritizes party over the founding document.

Their argument is about incentives rather than morality: elections punish behavior that voters object to, so where objection is replaced by indifference, norm-breaking becomes cheap. The authors point to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton — who challenged the 2020 election results and went on to win a 2026 Republican Senate primary — as their illustration of a candidate paying little electoral price. That is a contested reading of one race, and the broader claim that neutral voters are "complicit" is the authors' framing, not a measured finding. But the descriptive result is worth carrying around: when analysts report how many people support something alarming, the more revealing number is often how many declined to have a view.

related.title: Democratic Backsliding
related.hook: Democracies rarely die in a single coup anymore. More often they erode — legally, gradually, step by step — until little is left but the shell of elections.

related.title: Public Opinion & Polling
related.hook: What 'the people' think shapes what governments do — but measuring it is trickier than it looks, and a bad poll can mislead as easily as a good one informs.

related.title: Political Legitimacy
related.hook: Power can rest on fear alone, but it lasts when people believe it is rightful. That belief — legitimacy — is what separates authority from mere force.

related.title: Electoral vs Liberal Democracy
related.hook: Holding elections isn't the whole of democracy. Without rights, courts, and limits on the winner, voting alone can deliver an elected strongman.

flashcards.prompt: What do the authors mean by 'democratic neutrality'?
flashcards.back_html: Holding no opinion about politicians who undermine democratic norms — distinct from both supporting and explicitly opposing such behavior.

flashcards.prompt: Why do the researchers treat neutrality as more consequential than outright antidemocratic support?

choices.text: Because open support is rare (~8% on some items) while neutrality is widespread, and indifference removes the electoral penalty for norm-breaking
Because neutral respondents are more likely to run for office themselves
Because neutral voters turn out at much higher rates than partisans

flashcards.explanation_html: Explicit support polls in the single digits on some items; neutrality reaches around half. If breaking a norm costs no votes, there is little to deter it.

flashcards.prompt: How large was the evidence base for this finding?

choices.text: More than 48,000 Americans surveyed between September 2022 and July 2025
A single exit poll from one state election
A laboratory experiment with a few hundred students

flashcards.explanation_html: The authors pooled surveys fielded by YouGov, NORC and Bovitz across nearly three years, giving a sample of over 48,000.
